title: Why Save a History?
description: See why a shared project needs recoverable checkpoints before learning Git commands.

blocks.content:
Imagine you're writing a report and you accidentally delete a section that took hours to write. Without version control you have no way to get it back. Git solves this by saving **snapshots** of your project over time, so you can always go back to any earlier state.

Git is also **distributed** - every person working on a project has a complete copy of all the history on their own machine. You don't need a network connection to work, commit, or look at history.

## How Git Thinks About Your Project

Git sees your project in three areas:

```
Working Directory   -->   Staging Area   -->   Repository (History)
  (your files)         (changes ready          (saved snapshots /
                         to be saved)              commits)
```

- **Working Directory** - the folder on your computer where you edit files
- **Staging Area** - a holding zone where you collect changes before saving them
- **Repository** - the permanent record of every commit (snapshot) you've made

The typical flow is:
1. Edit files in your working directory
2. Stage the changes you want to save with `git add`
3. Save a snapshot with `git commit`

> A **commit** is a permanent snapshot. It stores what the project looked like at that exact moment, who made the change, when, and a message describing why.

blocks.question: What does Git give you when a teammate accidentally overwrites working code?
options: A history of saved snapshots you can restore from
An automatic backup uploaded to the cloud
A real-time sync of everyone's files
A lock that prevents two people editing the same file
blocks.explanation: Git keeps a permanent history of every commit. If something gets broken or overwritten you can look at the history and restore any earlier state. Git doesn't lock files or auto-sync - it tracks intentional snapshots.
